title: Binary Search & Pointer Tracking
description: How **Binary Search** uses Divide and Conquer to halve a sorted search space every step -- and how to track the `low`, `high`, `mid` pointers that make it work.

sections.title: Introduction to Binary Search
sections.content:
**Binary Search** finds a target in a **sorted array** without checking every element -- it finds the middle, compares, and throws away half the remaining data. Repeat.

Like flipping through a 1000-page dictionary: open to page 500, decide if your word comes before or after, and discard 500 pages instantly. Then 250. Then 125. Within 10 flips, you've found it.

Watch the analyzer trace this line by line and you'll see the required steps drop logarithmically with each division -- one of the most important scalable algorithms there is.

sections.title: Why Binary Search Matters
sections.content:
Search is everywhere -- every query, contact lookup, or product filter is a search under the hood.

At a billion records, linear search (up to 1 billion comparisons) stalls the processor. Binary Search, eliminating half the space per comparison, needs only ~30 -- the difference between a 30-second load and an instant response.
bullets: A clean demonstration of **Divide and Conquer**.

sections.title: The Absolute Requirement: Sorted Data
sections.content:
Binary Search **only works on sorted data** -- that's what makes the halving safe.

In `[2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12]`, if the target is 10 and the middle is 8, the target must be to the right -- guaranteed, since everything left of 8 is ≤ 8.

On unsorted data like `[10, 2, 8, 6, 12, 4]`, that guarantee vanishes -- the algorithm can discard the wrong half entirely and miss the target.

If your data is unsorted, sort it first (O(n log n)). One-off search? Plain linear search is faster. Searching many times? Sorting once pays off fast.

sections.title: The Core Idea of Binary Search
sections.content:
You don't need to read every element -- just narrow down where the target could be.

Loop:
1. Find the middle element.
2. Compare it to the target.
3. Discard the half that can't contain it (target < middle → discard right; target > middle → discard left).
4. Repeat on what's left.

Stop when found, or when the search space hits zero (return -1). Max steps for n elements: roughly log₂(n) + 1.

sections.title: Understanding the Search Pointers
sections.content:
Three pointers drive the search: **low** (start of the range), **high** (end of the range), **mid** (current middle, recalculated each step).

`low` starts at 0, `high` starts at `len - 1`. The loop runs while `low <= high` -- one element left means `low == high`; `low > high` means the search space is empty and the target isn't there.

Updating the pointers:
1. Target > mid → `low = mid + 1` (search right half).
2. Target < mid → `high = mid - 1` (search left half).
3. Get this math wrong (forgetting the +1/-1) and you'll trap the program in an infinite loop.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Pointer Execution
sections.content:
Searching for `11` in `[1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 15]`:

**Step 1:** low=0, high=6 → mid=3 (value 7). 11 > 7, discard left. `low = 4`. Remaining: `[9, 11, 15]`.

**Step 2:** low=4, high=6 → mid=5 (value 11). Match! Return index 5. Just 2 comparisons.

**Not-found example:** searching for `10` -- pointers eventually cross (`low` becomes 5, `high` becomes 4). Since `low > high`, the loop ends and returns -1.

From 7 elements, 2 comparisons. At 1 million elements, still only ~20.

sections.title: Why Binary Search Is Fast (Logarithmic Decay)
sections.content:
Every comparison removes 50% of what's left. At 1,000,000 elements: ~500,000 remain after 1 comparison, ~250,000 after 2, ~977 after 10, ~1 after 20.

At 1 billion elements, ~30 comparisons total -- versus linear search's up to 1 billion. That's **30 million times faster**. The O(log n) curve stays nearly flat while O(n) climbs steeply -- the gold standard for lookups.

sections.title: Python Implementation
sections.content: The iterative version is generally preferred in production -- O(1) memory, no recursion depth limit to worry about. The `while low <= high` condition is the whole engine: it stops automatically once the search space collapses.

sections.title: Recursive Binary Search & The Call Stack
sections.content:
Binary Search also works recursively -- instead of a `while` loop updating variables, the function calls itself with new `low`/`high` boundaries each time.

**Tracing a search for `9`** in `[1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 15]`:

* **Push:** `search(low=0, high=6)` → mid=3 (7). 9 > 7 → calls `search(4, 6)`.
* **Push:** `search(low=4, high=6)` → mid=5 (11). 9 < 11 → calls `search(4, 4)`.
* **Push:** `search(low=4, high=4)` → mid=4 (9). Match! Returns `4`.
* **Pop, pop, pop:** `4` flows back up through each frame to the caller.

Recursive versions use **O(log n) stack memory**; the iterative version stays at O(1).

sections.title: Complexity Analysis
sections.content:
**Time:** Best case **O(1)** (target is the very first middle checked). Average/worst case **O(log n)** -- max divisions to shrink to 1 element is log₂(n).

**Space:** Iterative -- **O(1)**, just three integers (`low`, `high`, `mid`) regardless of array size. Recursive -- **O(log n)**, one stack frame per call (~30 frames for 1 billion elements -- safe, but heavier than iterative).

sections.title: Binary Search vs Linear Search
sections.content:
**Linear Search:** works on unsorted data, O(n) time -- up to 1 billion ops at n=1 billion.

**Binary Search:** needs sorted data, O(log n) time -- ~30 ops at n=1 billion.

Two catches: **Sorting tax** -- unsorted data needs an O(n log n) sort first, so a single one-off search is actually faster with plain linear search. **Random access** -- binary search needs to jump straight to any index, which works great on arrays but fails on linked lists, where finding the middle means walking the whole list.

subsections.title: Limitations
bullets: Fails on structures without random access (linked lists).

sections.title: Real-World Applications
sections.content:
**Database Indexes (SQL):** B-Trees (a multi-branching binary search) locate rows instantly instead of scanning millions.

**`git bisect`:** mark a good and bad commit, and Git binary-searches your commit history, checking out the middle commit each round until it zeroes in on the exact commit that broke things.

**Search engines:** finding a keyword in a massive sorted inverted index is itself a binary search.

subsections.title: Mistake: Using Binary Search on chaotic arrays
subsections.content: Without sorted data, comparisons can't safely eliminate a half -- the algorithm can discard the correct half and return -1 even when the target's right there.

subsections.title: Mistake: Incorrect midpoint math
subsections.content: Use `//` not `/` in Python, or you'll get a non-integer index. In lower-level languages, `(low + high) / 2` risks integer overflow on huge arrays -- `low + (high - low) / 2` is the safer form.

subsections.title: Mistake: Infinite Pointer Loops
subsections.content: Write `low = mid` instead of `low = mid + 1` on a 2-element range, and mid keeps landing on the same index forever -- an infinite loop.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: Binary Search only works on **sorted data**.
It **halves the search space** every step.
Update with **`mid + 1` / `mid - 1`** to avoid infinite loops.
Iterative (O(1) memory) or recursive (O(log n) via the **Call Stack**).
